tool.name: Go
tool.tagline: Simple, fast compiled language for servers, tools and concurrent systems
tool.description: Go is a statically typed, compiled language from Google with a small spec, fast builds, garbage collection and first-class concurrency via goroutines and channels. It powers cloud infrastructure (Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform), web services and command-line tools. Learn it to build reliable, efficient networked software that is easy to read and deploy as a single binary.

glossary.def: The small file at the top of a Go project's folder that records the project's name, the Go version it needs and the other modules it uses.
The name you write in an import line to say which package you want, such as "fmt" or "example.com/shop/cart".
In Go, a name that starts with a capital letter (like Hello) is exported: other packages can use it. Lower-case names are unexported and stay private to their package.
Go's x := value form, which creates a new variable and sets it in one step, working out its type from the value. It only works inside functions.
The value a Go variable starts with when you don't set one: 0 for numbers, false for booleans, "" for text and nil for pointers, slices and maps.
The smallest piece of computer data: a single 0 or 1. Eight bits make a byte.
A named value that is fixed when the program is built and can never change while it runs, such as Pi = 3.14159.
A Go constant declared without a type, such as const Timeout = 5. It takes on whatever number type the place where it is used needs.
A Go word used inside a const group that counts the lines: 0 on the first, 1 on the next, and so on. It's how Go numbers a set of named choices.
A function that accepts any number of arguments of one type, such as sum(1, 2, 3) or sum(1). In Go it is written with ... before the type.
Handing a function a copy of a value, so changes the function makes to it don't affect the caller's original.
Go's everyday list type: a growable window onto an array of values of one type, written like []int.
Go's way of stopping a program when something has gone badly wrong, such as reading past the end of a list. It prints what happened and where, then exits unless the panic is recovered.
The Go pattern v, ok := ..., where the second result ok is true or false and says whether the lookup (a map key, a channel receive, a type check) actually found something.
Go's name for one character's Unicode number. A rune is stored as a 32-bit integer (int32).
Go syntax for writing a whole struct, slice or map value directly in code, like User{Name: "Ann"} or []int{1, 2, 3}.
The number that says where in memory a value is stored, like a house's street address.
To follow a pointer to the value it points at, to read or change that value. In Go you write *p.
The array that actually stores a Go slice's elements. Several slices can share one backing array.
The small record that is a Go slice: a pointer to its backing array, its length and its capacity. Passing a slice copies only this record, not the elements.
The value a Go method is called on, declared in brackets before the method name: in func (r Rect) Area(), r is the receiver.
All the methods a Go type has. A pointer type *T has both its own methods and T's, while T has only the methods declared on T itself.
Go syntax v.(T) that takes an interface value and gets back the concrete value of type T stored inside it, or reports that it holds something else.
A Go switch that branches on what concrete type an interface value holds: switch x := v.(type) { case int: ... case string: ... }.
A fixed error value a package shares so callers can check for it, such as io.EOF (end of input) or ErrNotFound.
Adding context to an error while keeping the original inside it, so the message says where it happened and code can still check for the original error.
A Go statement that schedules a function call to run when the surrounding function finishes, however it finishes. Used for clean-up such as closing files.
A function running independently, at the same time as the rest of a Go program. You start one by writing go before a call; they are cheap, so programs often run thousands.
A goroutine that waits forever for something that will never happen, so it never finishes and keeps holding memory until the program exits.
A Go pipe that goroutines use to pass values to each other safely: one sends a value in, another receives it out.
A Go channel with no storage: a send waits until another goroutine receives the value, so the two meet at that moment.
A Go channel with room to hold a few values, so sends don't wait until it's full and receives don't wait while it has values.
A Go statement that waits on several channel operations at once and runs whichever is ready first.
A Go counter (sync.WaitGroup) for waiting until a group of goroutines has finished.
A short note in backquotes after a Go struct field, like `json:"id"`, that tells packages such as encoding/json how to treat the field.
A Go struct field written as just a type, with no field name. The outer struct can then use the inner type's fields and methods directly.
A method of an embedded field that you can call directly on the outer Go struct, as if the outer struct had declared it.
In Go generics, the interface after a type parameter that says which types are allowed and what you may do with them, such as comparable or cmp.Ordered.
A Go constraint that lists the allowed types directly, such as ~int | ~float64.
The built-in type a Go named type is made from: for type Celsius float64, the underlying type is float64.
An iterator that drives the loop itself, handing each value to the loop body in turn. A pull iterator is the reverse: you ask it for the next value when you want one.
Spreading work from one channel across several goroutines that each take items from it, so a slow step runs in parallel.
Merging the output of several channels into one channel, so one reader can collect everything.
A fixed number of goroutines (workers) that take jobs from a shared channel, so at most that many jobs run at the same time.
A counter that limits how many tasks may do something at the same time; each task takes a slot before starting and gives it back when done.
A Go package (golang.org/x/sync/errgroup) that runs a group of tasks in goroutines, waits for them all, and returns the first error, cancelling the rest.
A Go testing tool (the -race flag) that watches a running program and reports when two goroutines touch the same data unsafely at the same time.
A guarantee that one operation's effects are visible to another: if A happens before B, B is sure to see everything A wrote.
Go's built-in profiling tool: it records where a program spends its time or memory and shows the results as lists, graphs and annotated code.
A Go tool that compares benchmark results from several runs and tells you whether a speed difference is real or just noise.
A chart of where a program spends its time: each function is a bar whose width shows its share, stacked on top of the function that called it.
The Go compiler's check of whether a value can stay in a function's own short-lived memory or must move to the heap because something still uses it after the function returns.
A compiler trick that copies a small function's code into the place that calls it, saving the cost of the call and opening up further speed-ups.
The Go setting for how many goroutines may run Go code at the same moment; it defaults to the number of CPU cores.
The Go setting that controls how often the garbage collector runs: how much memory may grow, as a percentage, before the next clean-up (default 100).
A Go setting that gives the program a soft memory ceiling; as memory use nears it, the garbage collector works harder to stay below.
The part of the Go runtime that decides which goroutine runs next, and on which operating-system thread.
A scheduling trick in which an idle worker takes waiting tasks from a busy worker's queue, so no processor sits idle.
The part of the Go runtime that waits for many network connections at once using the operating system's notification features, waking each goroutine when its data arrives.
Pausing a running task from outside so another can take a turn, even if the first never offered to stop.
A language's rules for when a write made by one thread or goroutine is guaranteed to be visible to another.
A garbage collection method: first mark every value the program can still reach, then sweep away (free) everything left unmarked.
A small piece of extra code the garbage collector adds to every pointer change while it is working, so it doesn't miss values the program is still using.
A short pause during which the garbage collector halts all of the program's code so it can do a step safely.
A table the Go runtime builds for each pairing of an interface and a concrete type, listing where to find that type's methods.
Copying a plain value into a separate spot in memory so it can be handled through a pointer, as Go does when an int or struct is stored in an interface.
The Go feature that lets Go code call code written in the C language, and the other way round.
The set of programs that turn source code into a running program — for Go, the go command with its compiler and related tools.
Go's rule for picking dependency versions: for each module, use the lowest version that satisfies every requirement, so builds come out the same every time.
A Go test style that lists many cases (inputs and expected results) in a slice and runs the same checks on each one in a loop.
A named test case run inside a Go test with t.Run, which reports separately and can be run on its own.
A measure of how much of your code actually ran during the tests, usually as a percentage of lines.
Automatically feeding a function huge numbers of generated, often strange, inputs to find ones that make it crash or misbehave.
A program examining its own values and types while it runs — for example listing a struct's fields and their names — instead of knowing them when it was written.
For a Go slice, how many elements fit in the array behind it before Go has to move everything to a bigger one; cap(s) reports it. For a channel, how many values it can hold waiting.

concepts.name: Running code with the go tool
concepts.summary: Install Go, write your first program, and use go run, go build, go fmt and go vet to run and check it.
concepts.why: Every Go task — running, building, tidying and checking your code — goes through the one `go` command, so it's the first thing to learn.
concepts.body:
A computer program is a list of instructions for a computer, written in a **programming language** such as Go. The text you write is called **source code**: ordinary text files, ending in `.go`, that people can read and edit.

A computer can't follow source code directly. A tool called a **compiler** first translates it into the computer's own instructions. Translating it like this is called **compiling** the program. The result is an **executable**: a file you can run, just like any app on your computer.

You drive Go from a **terminal**: a window where you type commands instead of clicking. After installing Go from go.dev/dl, type `go version` and press Enter; it should print something like `go1.23.4`. Every task is a word after `go`, such as `go run` or `go build`.

Go keeps each project in a **module**: a folder (also called a **directory**) containing a small file named `go.mod` that holds the project's name. Make a new folder, and inside it run `go mod init example.com/hello`; the name is only a label until you share your code. Save the example program as `main.go` in that folder. Then:

- `go run .` compiles the program in this folder and runs it straight away (the dot means "this folder"). It's what you'll use while learning.
- `go build` compiles it into an executable you keep, named after the module. You can copy that single file to another computer of the same kind and run it; nothing else needs installing.
- `go fmt ./...` is a **formatter**: it rewrites your files into Go's one standard layout of spaces and line breaks, so all Go code looks alike. Most code editors (the programs you write code in) run it every time you save.
- `go vet ./...` reads your code and points out likely mistakes that Go would otherwise allow.

Writing `./...` means "this folder and every folder inside it".

Go is strict on purpose. If your code brings in something it never uses, such as an unused `import` line (explained in the next lesson), the compiler stops with an error instead of a warning. Delete the unused line and run it again.
takeaways: `go mod init <name>` starts a project; `go run .` compiles and runs it
`go build` makes a single executable file you can copy and run
`go fmt` tidies the layout and `go vet` spots likely mistakes
pitfalls: Leaving an unused `import` line in your code — Go refuses to compile until you delete it.

quiz.q: You add `import "os"` to main.go but never use it. What happens when you type `go run .`?
options: Go stops with an error saying "imported and not used"
It runs and prints a warning
go fmt removes the import automatically before running
The unused line is silently ignored
quiz.explain: Go treats an unused import as an error, so it stops before running anything.

quiz.q: What does the compiler do when you run `go build`?
options: Checks your spelling and layout only
Uploads your code so others can use it
Translates your source code into an executable file the computer can run
Runs your program line by line without creating a file
quiz.explain: Compiling turns human-readable source code into an executable; go build saves that file for you.

concepts.name: Packages, imports and main
concepts.summary: How Go code is split into packages, how one file uses another package with import, and where a program starts.
concepts.why: Every Go file starts by naming its package, and which names other code may use depends entirely on packages.
concepts.body:
Programs grow to many files, so Go groups code into **packages**. A package is simply all the `.go` files in one folder. Every file starts with a line naming its package, such as `package greet`, and files in the same package can use each other's code freely.

Inside a file, code is organised into **functions**: named sets of instructions that run when you use the name. `func main() { ... }` defines a function called `main`, with its instructions between the curly braces. You'll write your own functions properly a few lessons from now.

The package named `main` is special: it becomes a program you can run, and its function `main` is the **entry point**, the place where the program starts. A package with any other name is a **library**: ready-made code for other packages to use.

To use another package you **import** it by its path: `import "fmt"`. Short paths like `"fmt"` (printing) or `"strings"` (working with text) belong to the **standard library**, the large collection of packages that comes with Go. Your own packages use the module name plus the folder, such as `"example.com/hello/greet"`. In your code you then write the package's name, a dot and the thing you want: `fmt.Println`, `greet.Hello`.

Everything you create gets a name — `Hello`, `shout`, `Total` — and its first letter decides who can use it:

- A name starting with a capital letter, like `Hello`, is **exported**: other packages can use it.
- A name starting with a lower-case letter, like `shout`, is unexported: only code in the same package can use it.

There are no special words such as `public` or `private`; the capital letter is the whole rule. It applies to everything you'll name: functions, fixed values, your own types and the parts inside them.

Two extras you'll meet in real projects. A folder named `internal` holds packages that only code from the same project may import. And a function named `init` runs automatically before `main`; it's handy for setup, but it hides when things happen, so use it rarely.
takeaways: One folder = one package; `package main` with `func main()` makes a runnable program
Capital first letter = usable from other packages; lower-case = private to its package
Import a package by its path, then use `name.Thing`
pitfalls: Trying to call a lower-case name like `greet.shout` from another package — the compiler won't allow it.

quiz.q: Package `greet` contains `func Hello()` and `func shout()`. Which can code in package main call?
options: Neither, unless main.go is in the greet folder
quiz.explain: Hello starts with a capital letter, so it's exported; shout is lower-case, so only code inside greet can use it.

quiz.q: What turns a package into a program you can run?
options: Naming it `package main` and giving it a `func main()`
Putting it in a folder called main
quiz.explain: Only package main builds into a program, and its main function is where the program starts.

concepts.name: Variables and basic types
concepts.summary: Store values in variables with var and :=, meet Go's basic types and zero values, and convert between types.
concepts.why: Go checks the type of every value before the program runs, which catches many mistakes early but means you convert between types yourself.
concepts.body:
A **variable** is a name that holds a value, like a labelled drawer. Every value has a **data type** (usually just called its type) that says what kind of value it is — a whole number, some text, true or false — and what you can do with it.

Go has two ways to create a variable:

- `var count int` creates `count` with the type `int`. `var name = "Ann"` lets Go work out the type from the value.
- `count := 0` is the **short declaration**: create the variable and set it in one step, with the type worked out for you. It only works inside functions, and it's the form you'll use most.

Once a variable has a type, it keeps it: `count` can never hold text. Go is **statically typed**, meaning the compiler checks every type before the program runs, so mix-ups are caught early.

A variable you don't set starts at its **zero value**: `0` for numbers, `false` for true/false, `""` (empty text) for text. A few types you'll meet later start as `nil`, Go's word for "nothing here".

The basic types:

- `int` holds an **integer** (a whole number) like 42 or -7. Sized versions such as `int8` and `int64` say how many **bits** (binary digits, 0 or 1) they use; plain `int` is the normal choice.
- `float64` holds a **floating-point number**, one with a decimal point, like 2.5.
- `bool` holds a **boolean**: `true` or `false`.
- `string` holds a **string**, a piece of text like `"hello"`.

Go never converts between types on its own, not even between `int` and `float64`. You do a **type conversion** by writing the type name like a function: `float64(n)` turns the whole number in `n` into a decimal one. Going the other way cuts off everything after the point: if `f` holds 2.9, `int(f)` is 2.

One catch: `:=` always makes a *new* variable. Inside an inner pair of braces `{ }`, such as the body of an `if` (next lesson), `x := 5` creates a second `x` that hides the outer one, and the outer `x` stays unchanged. To change an existing variable, use plain `=`.

While experimenting, `fmt.Printf("%T %v\n", x, x)` prints a value's type and the value itself.
concepts.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var total int // not set, so it starts at 0
	price := 2.5  // float64 (has a decimal point)
	qty := 3      // int (whole number)
	name, ok := "tea", true

	total = int(price * float64(qty)) // convert both ways explicitly
	fmt.Println(total, name, ok)      // 7 tea true

	var s string
	fmt.Printf("%q %T\n", s, qty) // "" int
}
takeaways: `:=` creates a variable inside functions; `var` when you want to name the type or start at zero
Every variable starts at a zero value such as 0, false or ""
Go never converts types for you — write `float64(n)`
pitfalls: Using `:=` inside the braces of an `if` or `for` when you meant to change an outer variable — it creates a new one instead.

quiz.q: Given `a := 7` and `b := 2.0`, which expression compiles?
quiz.explain: a is an int and b is a float64, so one must be converted; int(b) makes both whole numbers (Go has no type called float).

quiz.q: What value does `x` hold after `var x int`?
quiz.explain: Every variable starts at its type's zero value, and for int that's 0.

concepts.name: Constants and iota
concepts.summary: Name values that never change with const, let untyped constants fit where they're used, and number a set of choices with iota.
concepts.why: Constants give fixed values a clear name, and iota is how Go numbers a set of choices such as log levels or weekdays.
concepts.body:
Some values never change while a program runs: the number of days in a week, a tax rate, a greeting. Create them with `const` instead of `var`: `const Pi = 3.14159`. A **constant** is fixed when the program is compiled, and the compiler stops you if you try to change it.

Constants can be numbers, text, true/false values or single characters — not the bigger collections you'll meet in later lessons.

Most constants are **untyped**: `const Timeout = 5` has no fixed type until you use it. It becomes whatever type the place where it's used needs — an `int` here, a `float64` there — without a conversion. That's also why `time.Second * 5` works, even though `time.Second` has its own special type for lengths of time.

A typed constant, such as `const Max int32 = 100`, has a fixed type and follows the normal conversion rules.

Programs often need a short list of named choices — log levels `Debug`, `Info`, `Warn`, `Error` — where each name just needs a different number. Many languages call this an **enum**. Go has no special word for it. Instead, inside a `const ( ... )` group, the word **iota** stands for the line's position in the group: 0 on the first line, 1 on the next, and so on.

A line with only a name repeats the line above with the new iota. So `Debug Level = iota` followed by `Info`, `Warn` and `Error` gives 0, 1, 2 and 3. Starting the group with `_ = iota` throws away 0, which is useful when 0 should mean "not set".

The usual approach is to make your own type based on `int` — `type Level int` — and give the constants that type, so a level can't be mixed up with an ordinary number by accident. The example also gives `Level` a `String` function (a *method*, covered later) so levels print as words instead of numbers.

Go's enums aren't closed: `Level(42)` is accepted even though no name has that number. When a level comes from outside the program — typed by a user, read from a file — check that it's in range before using it.
takeaways: `const` names a value that's fixed when the program is compiled
Untyped constants take on the type they're used as
`iota` numbers the lines of a const group — Go's way to make enums
pitfalls: Assuming only the named values can exist — `Level(42)` is legal, so check values that come from outside.

quiz.q: In `const ( A = iota * 10; B; C )`, what is C?
quiz.explain: B and C repeat the expression `iota * 10` with iota 1 and 2, so C is 20.

concepts.name: if, for and switch
concepts.summary: Make decisions with if and switch, and repeat work with for, Go's only loop.
concepts.why: Almost every program must choose between actions and repeat steps; Go does both with just three keywords: if, for and switch.
concepts.body:
So far, code runs from top to bottom. **if** runs code only when a condition is true; this is called a **conditional**. `if age >= 18 { fmt.Println("adult") } else { fmt.Println("minor") }`. Go doesn't need brackets around the condition, but the curly braces are always required.

An `if` can start with a short setup step, followed by a semicolon: `if n, err := strconv.Atoi(s); err == nil { ... }`. Here `strconv.Atoi` turns text into a number and also returns `err`, which is `nil` when it worked — a habit you'll see everywhere. Variables made in the setup exist only inside that if/else. The part of the code where a name can be used is called its **scope**.

**for** is Go's only **loop**: code that repeats. Each pass through it is one **iteration**. It comes in a few shapes:

- `for i := 0; i < 10; i++ { }` — start `i` at 0, keep going while `i < 10`, add 1 (`i++`) after each pass.
- `for x < 100 { }` — repeat while a condition holds; `for { }` repeats forever until something stops it.
- `for i := range 10 { }` — count `i` from 0 to 9.
- `for i, v := range items { }` — go through a collection one element at a time, getting its position `i` and value `v`. Lists, text and maps all work this way (next lessons); write `_` for a part you don't need.

`break` leaves a loop early and `continue` jumps to the next iteration. To leave an outer loop from inside an inner one, put a label before the outer loop (`outer: for ...`) and write `break outer`.

**switch** compares one value with several options and runs the first that matches:

```go
switch day {
case "sat", "sun":
	fmt.Println("weekend")
default:
	fmt.Println("weekday")
}
```

Only the matching `case` runs: Go doesn't carry on into the next one, so no `break` is needed (the rare `fallthrough` word asks it to). One `case` can list several values, and `default` runs when nothing matches. A `switch` with no value, `switch { case x < 0: ... case x == 0: ... }`, is a tidy replacement for a long chain of if/else.
takeaways: `for` covers counting, while-style, endless and range loops
`if x, err := f(); err == nil { }` keeps short-lived variables inside the if
switch runs only the first matching case; one case can list several values
pitfalls: Writing `break` inside a switch inside a for loop to leave the loop — it only leaves the switch; use a label.

quiz.q: What does this print? `for i := range 4 { if i == 2 { continue }; fmt.Print(i) }`
quiz.explain: range 4 yields 0..3 and continue skips 2, printing 013.

concepts.name: Functions, multiple returns, closures
concepts.summary: Write your own functions, return several results (including an error), accept any number of arguments, and pass functions around.
concepts.why: Functions let you name a piece of work and reuse it, and returning a result plus an error is how every Go function reports failure.
concepts.body:
A function packages some steps under a name so you can run them whenever you need them, like a recipe. You've used `main` and `fmt.Println`; here's one of your own:

```go
func add(a, b int) int {
	return a + b
}
```

`a` and `b` are **parameters**: named inputs, each with a type (here they share `int`). The `int` after the brackets is the type of the result, and `return` hands the result back.

Calling `add(2, 3)` runs the function. The values you pass in, 2 and 3, are the **arguments**; the result it hands back, 5, is the **return value**.

Go functions can **return several values**. The universal convention is a result plus an error: `func parse(s string) (int, error)`. The caller receives both, `n, err := parse(s)`, and checks `err` first: `nil` means nothing went wrong. Use `_` to throw away a value you don't need.

Results can also be named, `func split(sum int) (x, y int)`. Named results start at their zero values, and a plain `return` sends them back. That's fine in short functions but hard to follow in long ones.

A **variadic** function accepts any number of arguments of one type: `func sum(nums ...int)`. Call it as `sum(1, 2, 3)`; inside, `nums` is a list (a slice, covered next). To pass a list you already have, write `sum(xs...)`.

Arguments are **passed by value**: the function gets its own copy, so changing a parameter doesn't change the caller's variable. (A slice, a map or a pointer, all coming soon, points at shared data, so changes made through it *are* seen by the caller.)

Functions are values too: you can store one in a variable, pass it to another function, or return it. A function written without a name, `func(x int) int { return x * 2 }`, can be created right where it's needed; this is an **anonymous function**. If it uses variables of the function around it it's a **closure**: it keeps those very variables (not copies) alive and shared, as `counter` in the example shows.

Go doesn't allow default values for parameters or two functions with the same name; give them different names instead.
takeaways: Return `(result, error)` and check the error where you call the function
A variadic `...T` parameter accepts any number of arguments
A closure keeps using the outer variables themselves, not copies of them
pitfalls: Ignoring a returned error by assigning it to `_` without a good reason.

quiz.q: `c := counter(); c(); c()` then `d := counter(); d()` — what does `d()` return (counter as in the example)?
quiz.explain: Each call to counter creates a new n, so d has its own counter starting from 0 and its first call returns 1.

concepts.name: Arrays and slices
concepts.summary: Keep lists of values in a fixed-size array or a growable slice, and use len, cap, append and slicing.
concepts.why: The slice is Go's everyday list type; almost every program uses it.
concepts.body:
Programs constantly deal with lists: scores, names, lines of a file. Go has two list types, and you'll mostly use the second.

An **array** holds a fixed number of values of one type, side by side: `[3]int` holds exactly three whole numbers. Each value sits at a numbered position called its **index**, counting from 0, so a three-element array has indexes 0, 1 and 2. Counting from 0 like this is called **zero-based indexing**. Read or change one element with `a[0]`.

The length is part of an array's type, so `[3]int` and `[4]int` are different types, and assigning an array copies every element. That makes arrays rigid, and you'll rarely use them directly.

A **slice**, written `[]int`, is the flexible list you'll use all the time. It's a window onto an array that Go manages for you, and it can grow. Make one from values, `[]int{1, 2, 3}`, or with `make([]int, 3)` for three zeros.

- `len(s)` is how many elements it holds. `cap(s)`, its **capacity**, is how many fit in the array behind it before Go needs a bigger one.
- `append(s, x)` adds `x` at the end and returns the updated slice. When there's no room, Go quietly copies everything into a bigger array. **Always store the result**: `s = append(s, x)`.
- A slice variable you haven't filled, `var s []int`, is `nil`, but behaves like an empty list: you can `append` to it straight away.
- Asking for `s[i]` past the end stops the program with an error. Go calls this kind of crash a **panic**.

Taking part of a slice is called **slicing**: `s[1:3]` gives the elements at indexes 1 and 2 — up to, but not including, 3. The part shares the same array as the original, so a change to one shows up in the other. Use `slices.Clone(s)` when you need an independent copy.

The standard `slices` package has ready-made helpers: `slices.Sort`, `slices.Contains`, `slices.Index`, `slices.Reverse`, `slices.Max`. Use them before writing your own loop.
takeaways: An array has a fixed size; a slice grows and is what you'll normally use
Always write `s = append(s, ...)`
A part taken with `s[a:b]` shares data with the original; use `slices.Clone` for an independent copy
pitfalls: Calling `append(s, x)` without storing the result — the new element is lost.

quiz.explain: b views a[1] and a[2]; b[1] is a[2], so a becomes [1 2 9 4].

quiz.q: What is `len(make([]int, 2, 10))`?
quiz.explain: make's second argument is the length; the third is capacity.

concepts.name: Maps
concepts.summary: Look values up by key with Go maps: add, read, change and delete entries, check whether a key exists, and loop over them.
concepts.why: A map is how you look something up by name — a phone book, word counts, settings — and it's built into Go.
concepts.body:
A slice finds things by position. Often you want to find them by name instead, the way a phone book takes you from a person to their number. A **map** stores **key-value pairs**: each key (the name) leads to one value (the number). `map[string]int` has text keys and whole-number values. Looking up a key stays fast however big the map gets.

Keys must be values Go can compare with `==`, such as numbers, text and true/false. A slice or a map can't be a key.

Create a map with some entries, `ages := map[string]int{"ann": 31}`, or empty with `make(map[string]int)`. A map variable that was never created is `nil`: reading from it is fine, but **adding to a nil map panics**, so always create the map first.

- `m[k] = v` adds an entry or replaces its value; `delete(m, k)` removes one (and does nothing if it isn't there); `len(m)` counts entries; `clear(m)` empties the map.
- `v := m[k]` gives the zero value when the key is missing. To tell "missing" apart from "present but zero", use the **comma-ok** form `v, ok := m[k]`: `ok` is `true` only when the key exists.
- Because missing keys read as zero, counting things is just `counts[word]++`.

`for k, v := range m` visits every entry, but in a **deliberately random order** that changes from run to run. When you need a fixed order, sort the keys first: `slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m))`.

Passing a map to a function doesn't copy it: the function works on the same map, so its changes stay. A map whose values don't matter, such as `map[string]bool`, is the usual way to keep a set of unique items. Maps aren't safe to change from several tasks running at the same time; the concurrency lessons show how to protect them.
takeaways: `v, ok := m[k]` tells a missing key apart from a zero value
Adding to a nil map panics — create it with `make` or `map[K]V{}`
Map order is random; sort the keys when you need a stable order
pitfalls: Expecting map entries to come out in the order you added them.

quiz.q: `var m map[string]int` — which statement panics?
quiz.explain: Reads, len and delete are safe on a nil map; assignment to a nil map panics.

concepts.name: Strings, bytes and runes
concepts.summary: How Go stores text as bytes, why one character can take several bytes, and the strings and strconv packages.
concepts.why: Counting, cutting and looping over text behaves surprisingly until you know that Go stores strings as bytes.
concepts.body:
Computers store everything as numbers, text included. The basic unit is a **byte**, a small number from 0 to 255. A Go string is a sequence of bytes holding text.

Once created, a string can't be changed: strings are **immutable**. Operations like `+` build a new string instead.

How do letters become numbers? The **Unicode** standard gives every character in every language its own number: `A` is 65, `é` is 233. Go stores those numbers as bytes using **UTF-8**, a scheme in which plain English letters take one byte and other characters take two to four.

That has two everyday consequences:

- `len(s)` counts bytes, not characters. `len("héllo")` is 6, because `é` takes two bytes.
- `s[i]` gives a single byte, and `s[a:b]` cuts by bytes, which can split a character in half.

A **rune** is Go's name for one character's Unicode number (its type is `int32`). Looping with `for i, r := range s` reads the text character by character: `i` is the byte position, `r` the rune. Use it whenever you mean "each character". `utf8.RuneCountInString(s)` counts characters, and `[]rune(s)` turns text into a slice of characters.

Because strings can't change, adding to one with `+=` inside a loop builds a whole new string every time. A `strings.Builder` collects the pieces efficiently instead. Convert text to bytes and back with `[]byte(s)` and `string(b)`; each conversion makes a copy.

The `strings` package covers most text work: `Contains`, `HasPrefix`, `Split`, `Fields` (split on spaces), `Join`, `Replace`, `ToUpper`, `TrimSpace`, `Cut`. For numbers written as text use `strconv`: `strconv.Itoa(42)` gives `"42"`, and `strconv.Atoi("42")` gives 42 plus an error. Careful: `string(65)` is `"A"`, the character numbered 65, not `"65"`.

Text written between backquote characters instead of double quotes is a **raw string**: backslashes stay exactly as typed, and it can span several lines. In double quotes, a backslash starts an **escape sequence**, such as `\n` for a new line.
takeaways: Strings are unchangeable sequences of UTF-8 bytes; `len` counts bytes
`range` over a string gives runes (characters); `s[i]` gives a byte
Build text with strings.Builder; convert numbers with strconv
pitfalls: Using `string(n)` to turn a number into text — use `strconv.Itoa(n)` or `fmt.Sprint(n)`.

quiz.q: What is the type of `c` in `for _, c := range "go"`?
quiz.explain: Looping over a string with range reads it character by character, giving runes.

concepts.name: Structs
concepts.summary: Group related values into a struct type of your own, create values of it, and copy and compare them.
concepts.why: Structs are how you describe your own kinds of data in Go — a user, an order, a point on a map.
concepts.body:
So far each variable holds one value. Real things have several details: a user has an ID, a name and an admin flag. A **struct** groups named values, called **fields**, into one new type:

```go
type User struct {
	ID    int
	Name  string
	Admin bool
}
```

`type User struct { ... }` creates a new type named `User`. To make a value of it, write a **composite literal**: the type name followed by field values in braces. Prefer naming the fields, `User{ID: 1, Name: "Ann"}`; fields you leave out get their zero values, and the code keeps working when fields are added later. The short form `User{1, "Ann", false}` must list every field in order, and breaks when the struct changes.

Read or change a field with a dot: `u.Name`, `u.Admin = true`. The capital-letter rule applies to fields too: upper-case fields can be used from other packages, lower-case ones can't.

Structs are copied as a whole. `v := u` copies every field, and passing `u` to a function hands it a copy, so changing the copy doesn't touch the original. To let a function change the original you'll use a pointer, in the next lesson. Two structs can be compared with `==` when all their fields can, which also lets them be map keys.

A struct can be written in place without a type name, `point := struct{ X, Y int }{1, 2}`, for one-off data. The empty struct `struct{}` has no fields and takes up no memory.

Many languages have special setup code, called a **constructor**, that runs whenever a value is created. Go doesn't. The convention is an ordinary function named like `NewUser` that checks its inputs and returns a ready-to-use value.
takeaways: Create structs with named fields, `T{Field: v}`; missing fields are zero
Assigning a struct copies it; use a pointer to share one
Structs whose fields can be compared support `==`
pitfalls: Using the short unnamed form `T{1, "x"}` for structs from other packages — it breaks when fields are added.

quiz.q: `a := Point{1, 2}; b := a; b.X = 9` — what is `a.X`?
quiz.explain: Assigning a struct copies it, so changing b leaves a untouched.

concepts.name: Pointers
concepts.summary: Use & to get a value's address and * to reach the value through it, so a function can change the caller's data.
concepts.why: Pointers decide whether a function works on a copy or on the original, and they're central to methods later on.
concepts.body:
While a program runs, its values live in the computer's **memory**, a long sequence of numbered storage slots. The number of a value's slot is its **memory address**, much like a house's street address.

A **pointer** is a value that holds an address. It tells you where another value lives, instead of being that value.

`&x` gives the address of `x`. If `x` is an `int`, `&x` has the type `*int`, read "pointer to int". Going the other way, `*p` means "the value at the address in `p`": reading or writing `*p` reads or writes `x` itself. Following a pointer like this is called **dereferencing** it.

Why bother? Go hands functions copies, so a function that must change its argument needs the argument's address:

```go
func reset(n *int) { *n = 0 }
reset(&count) // count is now 0
```

With structs Go saves you typing: if `p` is a `*User`, `p.Name` means `(*p).Name`. `&User{Name: "Ann"}` creates a struct and gives you its address in one step, and `new(T)` makes a zero-valued `T` and returns a pointer to it.

A pointer that points nowhere is `nil`, its zero value. Dereferencing a nil pointer makes the program panic: it stops with an error.

A function may safely return a pointer to one of its own variables: Go notices the value is still needed and keeps it. You never free memory yourself. The **garbage collector**, a part of Go that runs alongside your program, reclaims values once nothing points to them anymore.

Unlike some older languages such as C, Go doesn't let you do arithmetic on addresses, which rules out a whole family of memory mistakes.

When to use a pointer:

- A function must change the caller's value.
- The struct is large, and copying it on every call would be wasteful.
- You need a way to say "no value", using `nil`.

A slice or a map already refers to shared data, so you rarely need a pointer *to* one. For small structs you don't change, passing a copy is simpler and usually just as fast.
takeaways: `&x` gives an address, `*p` follows it; a pointer's zero value is nil
Pass a pointer when a function must change the caller's value
Returning a pointer to a function's own variable is safe; the garbage collector frees memory for you
pitfalls: Dereferencing a nil pointer — for example one you created but never pointed at anything.

quiz.q: `func f(u User) { u.Name = "x" }` is called as `f(user)`. What happens to `user.Name`?
quiz.explain: f receives a copy of the struct, so the caller's value is not modified.

concepts.name: Slice internals: append and aliasing
concepts.summary: How append grows the array behind a slice, when two slices share the same data, and how to avoid surprises.
concepts.why: Most confusing slice bugs come from not knowing when append reuses memory and when it copies.
concepts.body:
Behind the scenes a slice is a small record called the **slice header**: a pointer to the array that really holds the elements (the **backing array**), a length and a capacity. Passing a slice to a function copies this header, not the elements. So the function can change elements the caller sees — but if it appends, the caller's header still has the old length.

`append(s, x)` does one of two things:

- If `len(s) < cap(s)`, it writes `x` into the existing array and returns a header with a longer length. **Any other slice sharing that array sees the write.**
- Otherwise it allocates a new, larger array (roughly doubling for small slices, growing more gently for large ones), copies, and returns a header pointing to the new array. From then on, old and new slices are independent.

That's why this bug is so easy to write: take `a := base[:2]` from a slice of capacity 4, `append(a, 99)` — and you have silently overwritten `base[2]`. Defences:

- Use a **full slice expression** `base[:2:2]` to cap the capacity, forcing the next append to copy.
- Clone with `slices.Clone` before handing a slice to code that may append.
- If a function appends, return the new slice (`s = add(s, x)`) as `append` itself does.

When you know the final size, preallocate with `make([]T, 0, n)` to avoid repeated grow-and-copy cycles.

A small slice of a huge array keeps the whole array in memory, because the garbage collector can't free an array while any slice still points into it. If you only need a few bytes from a large buffer, copy them out instead of slicing.
concepts.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	base := make([]int, 4, 4) // [0 0 0 0]
	a := base[:2]             // len 2, cap 4
	a = append(a, 99)         // fits: writes into base[2]
	fmt.Println(base)         // [0 0 99 0]

	b := base[:2:2]   // len 2, cap 2
	b = append(b, 7)  // no room: copies to a new array
	fmt.Println(base) // [0 0 99 0] (unchanged)
	fmt.Println(b)    // [0 0 7]

	out := make([]int, 0, 3) // preallocate capacity
	for i := range 3 {
		out = append(out, i)
	}
	fmt.Println(len(out), cap(out)) // 3 3
}
takeaways: append writes in place while there's capacity, otherwise reallocates
`s[lo:hi:max]` limits capacity so append must copy
Preallocate with `make([]T, 0, n)` when the size is known
pitfalls: Appending to a sub-slice and unknowingly overwriting the parent's elements.

quiz.q: `s := make([]int, 3, 10); t := append(s, 1); u := append(s, 2)` — what is `t[3]`?
quiz.explain: Both appends fit in the same backing array and write index 3; the second write (2) overwrites the first, and t sees it.

concepts.name: Methods and receivers
concepts.summary: Attach methods to your types and choose between value and pointer receivers.
concepts.why: Methods give your types behaviour, and the receiver choice decides which interfaces a type satisfies.
concepts.body:
A **method** is a function attached to a type, called with a dot: `r.Area()`. It's declared like a function with one extra part before the name, the **method receiver** (usually just called the receiver):

```go
func (r Rect) Area() float64 { return r.W * r.H }
```

Inside the method, `r` is the value it was called on. You can define methods on any named type declared in the same package — structs, but also `type Celsius float64` or `type IDs []int`. You can't add methods to types from other packages; wrap them in a type of your own instead.

The receiver can be a value (`r Rect`) or a pointer (`r *Rect`):

- A **pointer receiver** is needed if the method changes the receiver. It's also better when the struct is large, or holds something that must never be copied, such as the `sync.Mutex` lock from the concurrency lessons.
- A **value receiver** works on a copy; it suits small types you don't change, like `time.Time` or a `Point`.
- Be consistent: if any method needs a pointer receiver, give them all pointer receivers.

Calls are convenient: on a variable `v`, `v.Scale(2)` automatically becomes `(&v).Scale(2)`, and a pointer is automatically followed for value-receiver methods.

The choice matters for **interfaces** (next lesson), which accept any type that has certain methods. All the methods a type has form its **method set**: `Rect` has only its value-receiver methods, while `*Rect` has both kinds. So if `Scale` has a pointer receiver, only `*Rect` — not `Rect` — counts as having `Scale`.

A nil pointer can still call a pointer-receiver method; the method just receives `nil`. Some types handle that on purpose, but usually it ends in a nil-pointer panic inside the method.

A method value, `f := r.Area`, ties the method to `r` so you can pass it around like any function.
takeaways: Pointer receivers to change the value or avoid copying; value receivers for small types you don't change
Methods can be declared on any named type in your package
Pointer-receiver methods are not in the value type's method set
pitfalls: Mixing value and pointer receivers on one type, then being surprised when T doesn't satisfy an interface.

quiz.q: `func (c Counter) Inc() { c.n++ }` — what does calling `c.Inc()` do to `c.n`?
options: Nothing; the method changes a copy
quiz.explain: A value receiver gets a copy of the struct, so the increment is lost.

concepts.name: Interfaces
concepts.summary: Describe behaviour as a set of methods that any type can satisfy, and get concrete values back with type assertions and type switches.
concepts.why: Interfaces let one function work with many different types; they're how your types plug into the standard library and how tests swap in fakes.
concepts.body:
An **interface** type is a list of methods — their names, inputs and results. Any type that has those methods satisfies it **automatically**; there's no `implements` keyword:

```go
type Shape interface { Area() float64 }
```

Every type with an `Area() float64` method is a `Shape`, even types written before the interface existed. So the code that *uses* a behaviour can declare the small interface it needs. Two Go sayings follow: "accept interfaces, return concrete types" (a concrete type is a real one, such as a struct), and keep interfaces small. The standard library's `io.Reader` (`Read(p []byte) (int, error)`), `io.Writer` and `fmt.Stringer` (`String() string`) have one method each, which is why so many types work with them.

An interface value holds two things: the concrete type stored in it and the value itself. `any` (another name for `interface{}`) has no methods, so it can hold anything — use it sparingly, because the compiler can no longer check what you do with the value.

To get the concrete value back:

- **Type assertion**: `s, ok := v.(fmt.Stringer)`. Without `ok`, a failed assertion panics.
- **Type switch**: `switch x := v.(type) { case int: ...; case string: ... }` — in each branch, `x` has that branch's type.

A frequent gotcha: an interface is `nil` only if both its type and its value are empty. Returning a nil `*MyErr` pointer as an `error` gives a non-nil interface, because the type part is filled in. Return a plain `nil` instead.

To have the compiler check that a type satisfies an interface, write `var _ Shape = (*Square)(nil)`.
takeaways: Types satisfy interfaces implicitly by having the methods
Keep interfaces small and define them where they are used
Use comma-ok assertions or type switches to recover concrete types
pitfalls: Returning a typed nil pointer as an interface — the interface is not nil.

quiz.q: Which types satisfy `interface{ Close() error }`?
options: Only types that declare they implement it
Only types in the same package as the interface
Any type with a method `Close() error`
quiz.explain: A type satisfies an interface automatically, just by having its methods.

quiz.q: What does `n := v.(int)` do if v holds a string?
quiz.explain: A single-result type assertion panics on mismatch; use `n, ok := v.(int)` to test safely.

concepts.name: Errors and wrapping
concepts.summary: Return errors as values, add context with %w, and inspect them with errors.Is and errors.As.
concepts.why: Explicit error handling is the most visible Go habit, and adding context to errors makes failures easy to trace.
concepts.body:
In Go an **error** is just a value implementing `interface { Error() string }`. Functions that can fail return it last, and callers check it immediately:

```go
f, err := os.Open(path)
if err != nil {
	return fmt.Errorf("load config: %w", err)
}
```

Handle each error once: either deal with it (try again, use a fallback value, or log it and carry on) or return it with added context. Don't log *and* return, or you'll see the same failure several times.

Creating errors:

- `errors.New("msg")` for a fixed message. Shared ones declared at the top level of a package are **sentinel errors**, like `io.EOF` or `var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")`.
- `fmt.Errorf("parse %q: %w", name, err)` adds context and wraps the original inside the new error — this is **error wrapping**. `%v` would only copy the text.
- A custom type (e.g. `type ValidationError struct{ Field string }` with an `Error` method) when callers need structured details.

Inspecting errors — always through the chain of wrapped errors, never by comparing strings:

- `errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound)` reports whether any error in the chain equals the target.
- `errors.As(err, &target)` finds the first error in the chain assignable to `target`'s type and stores it.
- `errors.Join(e1, e2)` combines several errors; `Is`/`As` search all of them.

Error strings are lower-case with no trailing punctuation, since they get prefixed: `open config: read file: permission denied`. Wrapping with `%w` lets callers depend on the inner error, so changing it later could break them; wrap deliberately.
takeaways: Return errors as the last result and check them right away
Wrap with `fmt.Errorf("context: %w", err)`
Use errors.Is for sentinels and errors.As for error types
pitfalls: Comparing `err.Error()` strings or using `==` on wrapped errors instead of errors.Is.

quiz.q: `err := fmt.Errorf("read: %v", io.EOF)` — what does `errors.Is(err, io.EOF)` return?
quiz.explain: %v only formats the text; without %w the original error isn't wrapped, so Is can't find it.

concepts.name: defer, panic and recover
concepts.summary: Schedule cleanup with defer, understand panics, and recover from them at boundaries.
concepts.why: defer is the standard way to release resources, and knowing panic/recover tells you when not to use them.
concepts.body:
A **defer** statement schedules a call to run when the surrounding function returns — normally, early, or by panic. Put it right after acquiring a resource so cleanup can't be forgotten:

```go
f, err := os.Open(name)
if err != nil { return err }
defer f.Close()
```

Rules worth knowing:

- Deferred calls run in **last-in, first-out** order.
- The arguments are **evaluated when the defer statement runs**, not when the call happens: `defer fmt.Println(i)` prints the value `i` had at that moment.
- Deferred closures can read and modify **named results**, which is how you can adjust the returned error after the fact.
- defer is per function, not per block. Deferring inside a long loop piles up calls until the function returns — move the loop body into a helper function.

A **panic** stops normal execution. Go runs the deferred calls of each function on the way out, and if nothing stops it, the program crashes and prints a stack trace (the list of function calls that led there). Mistakes found while running, such as following a nil pointer or an index past the end, panic, and you can call `panic(v)` yourself — but only for truly unrecoverable programmer errors or impossible states. Expected failures are errors, not panics.

**recover()** called inside a deferred function stops a panic and returns its value; elsewhere it returns nil. Use it at the edges of a program. For example, Go's built-in website support recovers from a panic in the code handling one visitor, so one bad page can't crash the whole site. Turn the recovered panic into an error. A panic in a goroutine — a function running at the same time as the rest of the program (covered in a later module) — can only be recovered inside that goroutine.
takeaways: defer cleanup right after acquiring the resource; deferred calls run last-in, first-out
Deferred call arguments are evaluated immediately
panic for bugs, errors for expected failures; recover only in a deferred func
pitfalls: Deferring Close inside a loop over many files — they all stay open until the function returns.

quiz.q: What does this print? `x := 1; defer fmt.Println(x); x = 2`
quiz.explain: The argument x is evaluated when the defer statement executes, when it is still 1.

concepts.name: Modules and go.mod
concepts.summary: Manage the code your project depends on with go.mod and go.sum, go get, go mod tidy, versions and workspaces.
concepts.why: Every real project depends on other modules, and the module system decides what code you actually build.
concepts.body:
A **module** is a set of packages released together under one version number, described by the `go.mod` file at its root:

```
module example.com/shop

go 1.23

require github.com/google/uuid v1.6.0
```

The `module` line is the start of the import path for your packages. The `go` line sets the minimum Go version. Since Go 1.21, if a module needs a newer version, the go command downloads that **toolchain** (the compiler and tools) automatically; a `toolchain` line can pin one.

Day-to-day commands:

- `go get example.com/lib@v1.4.0` adds or upgrades a **dependency**, another module your code uses (`@latest` for the newest release).
- `go mod tidy` adds missing requirements and removes unused ones. Run it before saving your changes to version control.
- `go list -m all` lists every module your build uses; `go mod why -m X` explains why X is needed.

`go.sum` records a fingerprint (a **hash**) of every module version used, so a tampered download is detected; commit it to version control too. Downloads go through Google's module mirror (proxy.golang.org) and are checked against a public database of those fingerprints.

Versions follow **semantic versioning**: numbers like v1.4.2, where a new first number signals changes that can break your code. To choose versions Go uses **minimal version selection**: for each module, the lowest version that satisfies every requirement. Builds are repeatable without a separate **lock file**. A new major version (v2 and up) must change the import path to `example.com/lib/v2`, so v1 and v2 can be used side by side.

When you work on several modules at once, `go work init ./app ./lib` creates a `go.work` workspace that builds them together; a `replace` line in go.mod points one dependency at a local folder instead. For private repositories, set `GOPRIVATE=github.com/yourorg/*` so Go fetches them directly instead of through the public mirror.
takeaways: go.mod declares the module path, Go version and requirements
`go mod tidy` keeps requirements accurate; commit go.mod and go.sum
Major versions v2+ live at a different import path (`/v2`)
pitfalls: Forgetting to commit go.sum, or editing go.mod by hand instead of using go get / go mod tidy.

quiz.q: Module A needs lib v1.2.0 and module B needs lib v1.4.0. Which version does Go select (v1.5.0 also exists)?
quiz.explain: Minimal version selection picks the lowest version that satisfies all requirements: v1.4.0.

concepts.name: Testing and table-driven tests
concepts.summary: Write tests with the testing package, organise them as tables with subtests, and run them with go test.
concepts.why: Go's built-in testing is used by every project; table tests are the house style.
concepts.body:
Tests live next to the code in files ending `_test.go`. A test is a function `func TestXxx(t *testing.T)` in the same package — or in a package named `pkg_test` if you want to test only what other packages can see. Run them with `go test ./...`; add `-v` to list each test, `-run 'Parse/negative'` to pick tests by name, `-cover` to see **code coverage** (how much of your code the tests ran), and `-count=1` to force a fresh run instead of reusing earlier results.

`*testing.T` reports failures:

- `t.Errorf(...)` records a failure and keeps going — preferred, so one run shows all problems.
- `t.Fatalf(...)` stops this test immediately — use it when continuing makes no sense.
- `t.Helper()` in helper functions makes failures point to the caller's line.
- `t.Cleanup(fn)`, `t.TempDir()` and `t.Setenv()` handle setting up and cleaning up.

The usual shape is a **table-driven test**: a slice of test entries, each with a name, inputs and expected output, run in a loop with `t.Run(tc.name, ...)`. Each one becomes a **subtest** that can be run alone and reports separately. Adding a case takes one line, which encourages covering unusual inputs.

Go's style is plain comparisons and clear messages — `got X, want Y` — rather than special assertion libraries. To compare whole slices or structs, use `slices.Equal`, `reflect.DeepEqual`, or a library that shows the differences, such as go-cmp.

`t.Parallel()` lets tests run at the same time as each other. Example functions (`func ExampleAdd()` with an `// Output:` comment) are compiled, run, and shown in the documentation. And `go test -fuzz` adds built-in **fuzzing**: Go generates random inputs to hunt for ones that break your code.
takeaways: Tests are `TestXxx(t *testing.T)` in `_test.go` files; run `go test ./...`
Table-driven tests + `t.Run` subtests are the usual structure
Prefer t.Errorf to keep going; t.Fatalf when you can't continue
pitfalls: Calling t.Fatal from a goroutine the test started (a function running separately, see the concurrency module) — it must be called from the test's own goroutine.

quiz.q: How do you run only the "negative" case of TestAbs?
quiz.explain: -run takes test names, with a slash between a test and its subtest; each part is matched as a pattern.

concepts.name: Goroutines
concepts.summary: Start work that runs at the same time as the rest of your program with the go keyword, and learn what goroutines are and cost.
concepts.why: Goroutines are the foundation of every concurrent Go program, from servers to pipelines.
concepts.body:
Normally a program does one thing at a time: a function call finishes before the next line runs. **Concurrency** means making progress on several tasks during the same period — serving many website visitors at once, say. In Go each such task is a **goroutine**: a function running independently of the rest of the program. Start one by putting `go` before a call: `go handle(conn)`. The call returns immediately, and the function carries on by itself.

Goroutines are cheap: each starts out using only a few kilobytes of memory, growing as needed. The Go **runtime** — code built into every Go program that manages it while it runs — shares goroutines out among a few operating-system **threads**, the units of work the computer actually runs side by side. So thousands, even hundreds of thousands, of goroutines are normal.

Things to keep in mind:

- When `main` returns, the program exits, **stopping any goroutines still running**. You must explicitly wait for work you care about, using channels or `sync.WaitGroup` (coming up).
- `go` throws away the function's return values. Results come back through channels or through shared variables protected by a lock.
- Goroutines share memory. If two of them use the same variable and at least one writes to it, they must take turns (synchronise); otherwise you have a **data race**, a bug whose result depends on timing.
- Since Go 1.22 each loop iteration gets its own copy of the loop variable, so `for _, url := range urls { go fetch(url) }` is safe. In older code you'll see `url := url` copies for this reason.

Every goroutine you start should have a clear way to finish. A goroutine stuck forever waiting on a channel nobody will send to is a **goroutine leak**: it holds its memory until the program exits. Think about who stops each goroutine before you write `go`.

`time.Sleep` to "wait for goroutines" only appears in toy examples; real code synchronises.
takeaways: `go f()` starts f concurrently and returns immediately
Goroutines are cheap, but the program exits when main returns
Every goroutine needs a defined way to finish
pitfalls: Starting goroutines in main and returning before they finish, so their work silently never happens.

quiz.q: main starts `go fmt.Println("hi")` and then returns immediately. What is printed?
options: Possibly nothing — main may exit before the goroutine runs
quiz.explain: Program exit doesn't wait for other goroutines, so the print may never happen.

concepts.name: Channels
concepts.summary: Pass values between goroutines with channels — unbuffered and buffered — and close them and loop over them.
concepts.why: Channels are Go's primary way for goroutines to communicate and synchronise.
concepts.body:
A **channel** is a typed pipe between goroutines: `ch := make(chan int)`. `ch <- v` sends a value in; `v := <-ch` receives one. Go's motto is *share memory by communicating*: pass data along instead of having goroutines change the same variables.

An **unbuffered channel** makes both sides meet: a send waits until a receiver takes the value, so it also tells the sender the value arrived. A **buffered channel**, `make(chan int, 10)`, has room for ten values: sends proceed until it's full, and receives proceed while it has values. Buffers smooth out bursts; they don't fix a design where nobody receives.

**Closing**: `close(ch)` tells receivers no more values are coming. After that, receives first get any values still waiting in the buffer, then return the zero value immediately; `v, ok := <-ch` gives `ok == false` once the channel is closed and empty. `for v := range ch` loops until the channel is closed and empty — the standard receiving loop. Rules:

- Only the **sender** closes, and only when receivers need to know it's done. Not every channel needs closing.
- Sending on a closed channel panics; closing twice panics.
- A nil channel waits forever on both send and receive.

Direction can be part of the type, and the compiler enforces it: `chan<- int` can only send, `<-chan int` can only receive. Functions that produce values usually return `<-chan T`.

If every goroutine is stuck waiting on a channel, the runtime stops the program with `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!`. That's a **deadlock**, and the most common first channel bug, usually a send that nobody receives.
takeaways: Unbuffered channels make sender and receiver meet; buffered ones queue values
The sender closes; receivers use `range` or `v, ok := <-ch`
Use direction in types, `<-chan T` / `chan<- T`, to document intent
pitfalls: Closing a channel from the receiver side or from several senders — causes send-on-closed panics.

quiz.q: What happens when you receive from a closed, empty `chan int`?
options: It returns the last value sent
quiz.explain: Receiving from a closed channel never waits; once any buffered values are used up, it returns the zero value with ok == false.

concepts.name: select and timeouts
concepts.summary: Wait on several channel operations at once, add timeouts, and send or receive without waiting.
concepts.why: select is how goroutines react to whichever event comes first: data, cancellation or a deadline.
concepts.body:
A **select** statement waits on several channel operations and runs the case for whichever is ready first:

```go
select {
case msg := <-inbox:
	handle(msg)
case out <- next:
	sent++
case <-quit:
	return
}
```

If several are ready at once, select picks one **at random**, so no channel gets ignored forever. If none is ready, it waits.

Common patterns:

- **Timeouts** (a limit on how long to wait): add `case <-time.After(2 * time.Second):` to give up waiting. In a long-running loop, prefer one `time.NewTimer` or a context deadline, because each `time.After` call creates a new timer.
- **Operations that don't wait**: a `default` case runs immediately when nothing else is ready. `select { case ch <- v: default: dropped++ }` sends if possible and drops otherwise.
- **Cancellation**: include `case <-ctx.Done():` (next lessons) so a goroutine stops when its work is no longer wanted.
- **Event loops**: `for { select { ... } }` is the standard shape for a goroutine that serves several channels.

A nil channel is never ready, which is a useful trick: set a channel variable to `nil` to disable its case once it's closed, while still serving the others.

An empty `select {}` blocks forever. And a `default` case inside a `for` loop makes the loop spin without pausing, keeping a CPU core fully busy — only use `default` when you genuinely have something else to do.
takeaways: select runs the first ready case; ties are broken randomly
`time.After` or a context gives you timeouts
`default` lets an operation go ahead without waiting — avoid it in tight loops
pitfalls: Using an unbuffered result channel with a timeout: when the timeout wins, the sender blocks forever and leaks.

quiz.q: In the example, why is slowQuery's channel buffered with capacity 1?
options: So the goroutine can send and exit even if nobody receives after the timeout
quiz.explain: If the caller stopped waiting, an unbuffered send would block forever and leak the goroutine.

concepts.name: sync.WaitGroup and Mutex
concepts.summary: Wait for a group of goroutines, protect shared state with Mutex and RWMutex, and run setup once.
concepts.why: Not everything fits channels; WaitGroup and Mutex are the simplest correct tools for many jobs.
concepts.body:
**sync.WaitGroup** waits for a set of goroutines to finish:

- `wg.Add(n)` before starting the goroutines (in the launching goroutine, not inside the new one).
- `defer wg.Done()` at the top of each goroutine.
- `wg.Wait()` blocks until the counter reaches zero.

(Go 1.25 adds `wg.Go(f)`, which does the Add/Done bookkeeping for you.)

**sync.Mutex** is a **mutex** (short for mutual exclusion): a lock only one goroutine can hold at a time. Call `mu.Lock()`, then `defer mu.Unlock()`. Keep the mutex in the same struct as the data it protects, and keep the locked section short — never hold a lock while waiting on a file, the network or a channel. **sync.RWMutex** allows many readers at once (`RLock`) or one writer (`Lock`); it only pays off when reads far outnumber writes.

Other useful pieces:

- `sync.Once` (or `sync.OnceValue`, Go 1.21+) runs initialisation exactly once, even with concurrent callers.
- `sync/atomic` types such as `atomic.Int64` for simple counters and flags; each update happens as one indivisible step.
- `sync.Map` for some special kinds of cache; a plain map plus a mutex is usually clearer.

A mutex or WaitGroup **must not be copied** after first use. Pass structs containing them by pointer and use pointer receivers; `go vet` flags copies.

When should you use a mutex instead of a channel? Use channels to pass ownership of data or coordinate stages of work; use a mutex when goroutines simply need safe access to a shared structure such as a cache or counter.
takeaways: WaitGroup: Add before `go`, `defer Done()` inside, Wait to join
Keep the Mutex next to the data it guards; lock briefly
Never copy a Mutex or WaitGroup — use pointers
pitfalls: Calling wg.Add(1) inside the goroutine, racing with wg.Wait().

quiz.q: Why is `Record` declared with a pointer receiver?
options: A value receiver would lock a copy of the mutex, so nothing would be protected
Maps can't be used with value receivers
quiz.explain: With a value receiver each call copies the struct, including its Mutex, so the lock guards nothing shared.

concepts.name: context: cancellation and deadlines
concepts.summary: Pass cancellation, timeouts and per-request values down through your function calls with context.Context.
concepts.why: Every server, client and long-running operation in Go is expected to accept a context and stop when it's done.
concepts.body:
A **context.Context** travels from function to function carrying three things: a cancellation signal ("stop, this work is no longer wanted"), an optional deadline, and a few values that belong to one request. By convention it is the **first parameter**, named `ctx`: `func Fetch(ctx context.Context, url string) error`.

Contexts form a tree. Start from `context.Background()` (in main, tests, top-level) and derive children:

- `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(parent)` — cancelled when you call `cancel()`.
- `context.WithTimeout(parent, 2*time.Second)` / `WithDeadline` — cancelled automatically at the deadline.
- Cancelling a parent cancels all its children.

**Always `defer cancel()`** right after creating a derived context; it frees the context's timer and other resources even when the work finishes early. `go vet` warns if you forget.

Code doing the work checks for cancellation:

- `<-ctx.Done()` is a channel that closes on cancellation — use it in a `select`.
- `ctx.Err()` then returns `context.Canceled` or `context.DeadlineExceeded`.
- Pass `ctx` on to everything that blocks: `http.NewRequestWithContext`, database queries, your own functions.

`context.WithValue` attaches data that belongs to one request, such as a trace ID (a label that ties together all the log lines of that request). Use an unexported key type so different packages' keys can't clash. Don't use it to pass optional function parameters.

Don't store contexts in structs; pass them explicitly. Use `context.TODO()` as a placeholder when you haven't plumbed one through yet. Go 1.21 added `context.WithoutCancel` and `context.AfterFunc` for advanced uses.
takeaways: Pass `ctx context.Context` as the first parameter, never store it
Derive with WithCancel/WithTimeout and always `defer cancel()`
Blocking code selects on `ctx.Done()` and returns `ctx.Err()`
pitfalls: Ignoring ctx inside a loop or blocking call, so cancellation never actually stops the work.

quiz.q: A parent context is cancelled. What happens to a child created with context.WithTimeout(parent, time.Hour)?
options: It keeps running until its hour is up
quiz.explain: Cancellation propagates from parent to all derived children, regardless of their own deadlines.

concepts.name: JSON and struct tags
concepts.summary: Encode and decode JSON with encoding/json, control field names with struct tags, and stream data.
concepts.why: JSON is the common format of web APIs and config files, and struct tags are how Go matches it to your types.
concepts.body:
The `encoding/json` package converts Go values to JSON text and back, which is called **serialization** (Go names the two directions marshal and unmarshal):

- `json.Marshal(v)` returns `[]byte`; `json.MarshalIndent` pretty-prints.
- `json.Unmarshal(data, &v)` decodes into a pointer.
- `json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v)` and `json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(&v)` stream to and from any `io.Writer` / `io.Reader`, such as the body of a web request.

Only **exported** fields are encoded; lower-case fields are silently ignored — the classic "my JSON is `{}`" bug. **Struct tags** customise the mapping:

```go
type User struct {
	ID       int    `json:"id"`
	Email    string `json:"email,omitempty"`
	Password string `json:"-"`
}
```

- `json:"name"` sets the key; `-` skips the field.
- `omitempty` drops zero values (empty string, 0, nil, empty slice or map). It doesn't treat an empty struct as empty. Newer Go versions (1.24+) add `omitzero` for that.
- Matching on decode is case-insensitive, and unknown keys are ignored unless you call `dec.DisallowUnknownFields()`.

Type mapping: objects decode into structs or `map[string]any`, arrays into slices, numbers into any numeric field — and into `float64` when the target is `any`. Use a pointer field (`*int`) when you must distinguish "missing" from zero. `time.Time` becomes text like `"2024-05-01T10:00:00Z"`.

For custom formats, implement `MarshalJSON`/`UnmarshalJSON`, or `encoding.TextMarshaler` for values that are naturally strings. `json.RawMessage` keeps part of a document as raw bytes to decode later.
takeaways: Only exported fields are (un)marshalled
Struct tags set names: `json:"name,omitempty"`, `json:"-"`
Use Decoder/Encoder for streams like HTTP bodies
pitfalls: Passing a value instead of a pointer to json.Unmarshal — it returns an InvalidUnmarshalError.

quiz.q: A struct has field `count int` with tag `json:"count"`. What does Marshal output for it?
options: Nothing; the field is unexported so it's skipped
quiz.explain: encoding/json ignores unexported fields even if they have a tag.

concepts.name: HTTP servers and clients
concepts.summary: Build an HTTP API with net/http's ServeMux routing patterns and call services with a configured client.
concepts.why: net/http is ready for real-world use; many Go services need nothing else for HTTP.
concepts.body:
`net/http` contains both a web **server** and an HTTP **client**.

**Server.** A **request handler** is the code that answers one incoming request: anything with a method `ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request)`, where `w` is where you write the **response** and `r` describes the request. Usually you register plain functions on a `*http.ServeMux`, Go's router, which picks the handler from the request's path. Since Go 1.22 patterns can include the HTTP method and wildcards (placeholders in braces):

- `mux.HandleFunc("GET /items/{id}", getItem)` — read the wildcard with `r.PathValue("id")`.
- `"POST /items"` matches only POST; a request with another method automatically gets the **status code** 405 Method Not Allowed.
- `"/static/"` with a trailing slash matches everything below it; `{path...}` captures the rest of the path.

In a handler, set headers with `w.Header().Set(...)` **before** `w.WriteHeader(status)` or the first `Write`. `r.Context()` is cancelled when the client disconnects. Each request runs in its own goroutine, so shared data needs a mutex or similar.

**Middleware** — code that wraps a handler to add logging, login checks or panic recovery — is just a function `func(http.Handler) http.Handler`.

Use an explicit `http.Server` with timeouts rather than `http.ListenAndServe`, which has none; otherwise slow clients can hold connections open forever. For a **graceful shutdown**, call `srv.Shutdown(ctx)` when the program receives SIGTERM, the operating system's polite "please stop" signal.

**Client.** `http.Get` uses `http.DefaultClient`, which has **no timeout**. Create a client with `&http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}` and reuse it — it keeps connections open and reuses them. Build requests with `http.NewRequestWithContext`, always `defer resp.Body.Close()`, and check `resp.StatusCode`: a 404 or 500 is not an error.

`net/http/httptest` lets you test handlers without a network (`httptest.NewRecorder`) or start a real server just for a test.
takeaways: Go 1.22+ ServeMux patterns: `"GET /items/{id}"` + `r.PathValue`
Set server and client timeouts; the defaults have none
Always close resp.Body and check StatusCode yourself
pitfalls: Calling w.Header().Set after w.WriteHeader or Write — the header is already sent and the change is ignored.

quiz.q: `resp, err := client.Get(url)` returns a 500 response. What is err?
options: nil — HTTP error statuses are not Go errors
quiz.explain: The client returns an error only when the request couldn't be sent or the reply couldn't be read, such as a network failure; you must check resp.StatusCode yourself.

concepts.name: Embedding and composition
concepts.summary: Build types out of other types with embedded fields and interfaces, and understand promoted methods and their limits.
concepts.why: Go has no inheritance (one type automatically extending another); embedded fields are how you reuse behaviour and build bigger interfaces from small ones.
concepts.body:
A struct can **embed** another type by listing it without a field name:

```go
type Logger struct{ prefix string }
func (l *Logger) Log(msg string) { fmt.Println(l.prefix + msg) }

type Service struct {
	*Logger
	name string
}
```

The embedded type's fields and methods are **promoted**: `svc.Log("hi")` works as if `Service` had declared `Log` itself, and `Service` now satisfies any interface that `Log` helps satisfy. The embedded value is still an ordinary field, named after its type: `svc.Logger`.

This is composition — building a type from parts — not **inheritance**:

- A promoted method still runs on the inner value. Inside `Log`, `l` is the `*Logger`, which knows nothing about the outer `Service`. If `Log` calls another method, it calls the `Logger` one; Go never redirects the call to a same-named method of the outer type.
- An outer method or field with the same name hides the promoted one; you can still reach it as `svc.Logger.Log`.
- If two embedded types at the same level provide the same name, using that name is a compile error, because Go can't tell which you mean — but only if you actually use it.

**Interfaces can embed interfaces** to build larger ones: `io.ReadWriter` is `interface{ Reader; Writer }`.

Embedding an **interface in a struct** is a handy wrapping trick: the struct satisfies the whole interface, and you write only the methods you want to change. Tests, and wrappers that add behaviour such as logging or counting, use it often — but if the embedded interface is nil, calling a method you didn't write panics.

Be careful in exported structs: every promoted method becomes part of your package's public API. Embedding a `sync.Mutex` there, for example, lets any user call `Lock` and `Unlock`.
takeaways: Methods of embedded fields are promoted to the outer type
Promoted methods only see the inner value — calls are never redirected to the outer type
Embed interfaces to combine them, or to wrap a value and change only some methods
