pitfalls: Embedding a type in an exported struct and accidentally exposing its methods (e.g. Lock/Unlock) as API.

quiz.q: Service embeds *Logger whose Log method calls l.Prefix(). Service also defines its own Prefix(). Which Prefix runs when you call svc.Log()?
quiz.explain: Inside Log the receiver is the *Logger, so it calls Logger.Prefix; Go never redirects the call to the outer type's method.

concepts.name: Generics: type parameters
concepts.summary: Write functions and types with type parameters, and limit them with constraints like comparable and cmp.Ordered.
concepts.why: Generics let one function or type work for many types, without copy-paste and without losing the compiler's type checks.
concepts.body:
Since Go 1.18, functions and types can take **type parameters** in square brackets: placeholders for types that the caller fills in. This is Go's version of **generics**:

```go
func Map[T, U any](xs []T, f func(T) U) []U
```

Each type parameter has a **type constraint**: an interface saying which types are allowed and what you may do with them:

- `any` — no requirements; you can only move and store values.
- `comparable` — supports `==` and `!=`, required for map keys.
- `cmp.Ordered` — supports `<`, `>`; covers integers, floats and strings.
- Your own: `type Number interface { ~int | ~int64 | ~float64 }`. A **type set** like this lists permitted types; `~int` means "any type whose **underlying type** (the built-in type it's made from) is int", so a `type Celsius int` qualifies too. Constraints can also require methods.

Callers rarely write type arguments: in `Map(nums, strconv.Itoa)` the compiler works out `T` and `U` itself (**type inference**). You need explicit arguments only when inference has nothing to go on, such as `Zero[int]()`.

Generic types work the same way: `type Stack[T any] struct{ items []T }`, with methods `func (s *Stack[T]) Push(v T)`. Methods cannot introduce *new* type parameters of their own — write a top-level function instead.

When to use them: containers, and algorithms over slices, maps and channels (the `slices` and `maps` packages are generic). When not to: if an ordinary interface with methods expresses the behaviour, prefer it. A good rule is to write the concrete code first and introduce type parameters when you find yourself duplicating it for several types.

Inside generic code you can't use a type switch on `T` directly; you'd convert to `any` first, which is a sign generics may be the wrong tool.
takeaways: Type parameters go in brackets with a constraint: `[T cmp.Ordered]`
`~T` in a constraint admits types with underlying type T
Type arguments are usually inferred from the call
pitfalls: Reaching for generics where a plain interface with methods is simpler and clearer.

quiz.q: `type Celsius float64`. Which constraint lets `Sum[Celsius]` compile?
quiz.explain: `~float64` includes every type whose underlying type is float64; plain `float64` admits only float64 itself.

concepts.name: Range-over-func iterators
concepts.summary: Write and consume Go 1.23 iterators: iter.Seq, iter.Seq2, yield, and the iterator helpers in slices and maps.
concepts.why: Iterators give custom collections and lazy sequences the same `for range` syntax as slices and maps.
concepts.body:
Go 1.23 lets `for range` loop over **functions**. An **iterator** here is a function that takes a `yield` **callback** — a function handed to it — and calls it once per element:

```go
func(yield func(V) bool)       // iter.Seq[V]
func(yield func(K, V) bool)    // iter.Seq2[K, V]
```

The `iter` package names these types. When you write `for v := range seq { ... }`, the compiler turns the loop body into the `yield` function. `yield` returns `false` when the loop stops early (via `break`, `return` or a panic), and the iterator **must** stop calling it then — calling yield after it returned false panics at run time. The standard shape is:

```go
if !yield(v) { return }
```

These are **push iterators**: the sequence drives the loop, pushing each value into it. `iter.Pull` turns one into a pull-style pair of functions, `next()` and `stop()`, for when you need to step through two sequences side by side, one element from each at a time; always call `stop` when done.

The standard library embraces them:

- `slices.All`, `slices.Values`, `slices.Backward`, `slices.Collect`, `slices.Sorted`.
- `maps.Keys`, `maps.Values`, `maps.All`, `maps.Collect`.
- Go 1.24 added `strings.Lines`, `strings.SplitSeq` and friends.

Iterators are **lazy**: nothing is computed until the loop asks for it, so infinite sequences and pipelines that stop early are cheap. Their natural partner is generics: functions like `Filter[V any](seq iter.Seq[V], keep func(V) bool) iter.Seq[V]` compose cleanly.

A method that returns an iterator is conventionally named `All`, or after what it yields (`Keys`, `Lines`). Most iterators can be ranged over more than once; document it if yours can't.
takeaways: `iter.Seq[V]` is `func(yield func(V) bool)`; range over it directly
Stop as soon as yield returns false
slices and maps provide All/Values/Keys/Collect/Sorted helpers
pitfalls: Ignoring yield's return value — breaking out of the loop then causes a runtime panic.

quiz.q: A consumer `break`s out of `for v := range seq`. What does seq's yield call return at that point?
quiz.explain: yield returns false when the loop body stops early; the iterator must then return without calling yield again.

concepts.name: Concurrency patterns: pipelines and fan-out
concepts.summary: Compose goroutines and channels into pipelines, fan-out/fan-in, and cancellable stages with errgroup.
concepts.why: Real concurrent programs are built from a few well-known patterns, which also make sure every goroutine finishes.
concepts.body:
A **pipeline** is a series of stages connected by channels, like an assembly line. Each stage is a function that receives values from an input channel, processes them, and sends to an output channel it owns and closes:

```go
func square(ctx context.Context, in <-chan int) <-chan int
```

Two rules keep pipelines correct:

- **The stage that creates a channel closes it**, with `defer close(out)` in its goroutine, so downstream `range` loops end.
- **Every send also selects on `ctx.Done()`**. If the consumer quits early, upstream goroutines must be able to give up instead of blocking forever on a send — otherwise they leak.

**Fan-out** means starting several goroutines reading from the same input channel, so a slow stage works on several items at once; each value goes to whichever goroutine receives it first. **Fan-in** (merge) combines several channels into one: start a goroutine per input that forwards values, and a final goroutine that waits on a WaitGroup and closes the output.

For the very common "run N tasks concurrently, stop on first error" case, use the **errgroup** package, `golang.org/x/sync/errgroup`:

- `g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)`; `g.Go(func() error {...})` for each task.
- The first error cancels `ctx`, so sibling tasks can stop early; `g.Wait()` returns that error.
- `g.SetLimit(n)` allows at most n tasks to run at once.

A **semaphore** — a buffered channel of capacity n where you send to acquire and receive to release — is the simplest way to cap parallelism by hand.

Ordering is lost once you fan out. If results must stay in input order, carry an index with each item and reassemble, or write results into a preallocated slice at that index.
takeaways: Each stage owns and closes its output channel
Every blocking send also selects on ctx.Done() to prevent leaks
errgroup covers run-N-tasks-and-stop-on-first-error
pitfalls: A consumer that stops reading early without cancelling, leaving upstream goroutines blocked forever.

quiz.q: In a fan-in merge of three input channels, when is it safe to close the output channel?
options: Right after starting the forwarding goroutines
Never; output channels must not be closed
After all forwarding goroutines have finished (WaitGroup.Wait)
quiz.explain: Closing earlier would make a still-running forwarder send on a closed channel and panic.

concepts.name: Worker pools and rate limiting
concepts.summary: Cap how much runs at once with a fixed pool of workers reading a job channel, collect results and errors, and pace the work.
concepts.why: An unlimited number of goroutines can use up memory or open files, or swamp a service you call; a pool keeps the load predictable.
concepts.body:
Starting one goroutine per item is fine for a hundred items, but not for a million URLs or rows, and it can overwhelm whatever you're calling. A **worker pool** fixes concurrency at N:

1. Create a `jobs` channel and a `results` channel.
2. Start N worker goroutines, each running `for j := range jobs { results <- process(j) }`.
3. Feed jobs from another goroutine and `close(jobs)` when done — this is what ends the workers' loops.
4. When all workers have returned (a WaitGroup), close `results` so the collector's `range` ends.

Choose N based on what limits the work. For **CPU-bound** work (limited by computation), use about the number of CPU cores, `runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0)`. For **I/O-bound** work (mostly waiting on the network or disk), use what the other system can handle, often a few tens.

Carry errors in the result type (`type result struct { id int; err error }`) rather than dropping them, and decide whether one failure should cancel the rest — if so, use a context or `errgroup` with `SetLimit(n)`, which is effectively a worker pool with error handling built in.

To limit **rate** rather than concurrency, use a `time.Ticker` to pace job submission, or `golang.org/x/time/rate.Limiter`, which hands out a fixed number of permits per second; its `Wait(ctx)` waits until the next request is allowed.

Size channel buffers deliberately. A buffered `jobs` channel lets the producer run ahead; an unbuffered one gives natural back-pressure, because the producer must wait until a worker is free. Large buffers mostly hide problems.

Remember results arrive in completion order, not submission order; include an id if the caller needs to match them up.
takeaways: N workers ranging over a jobs channel bound concurrency to N
Close jobs to stop workers; close results after wg.Wait()
Use rate.Limiter or a Ticker when the limit is requests per second
pitfalls: Closing the results channel from a worker, or before all workers finish — causes a send-on-closed panic.

quiz.q: In the example, what would happen if `close(jobs)` were removed?
options: Workers exit after the last job anyway
Workers block forever, wg.Wait never returns, and main deadlocks
Results are lost but the program exits
quiz.explain: Workers' range loops only end when jobs is closed; without it results is never closed and main's range blocks.

concepts.name: Data races and the race detector
concepts.summary: What a data race is, why it makes program behaviour unpredictable, and how go test -race finds races.
concepts.why: Races cause rare bugs that are hard to reproduce in production; the race detector catches most of them during testing.
concepts.body:
A **data race** happens when two goroutines use the same variable at the same time, at least one of them writes, and nothing makes them take turns (no mutex, channel or atomic operation). Races cause more than lost updates. To run fast, the compiler and the processor may reorder memory operations or keep private copies of values, so another goroutine can see stale data.

Values made of several parts — a string, slice, interface or map — can even be seen half-written, which leads to crashes. Two goroutines writing to one map at once stop the program with a fatal error.

Go ships a **race detector**. Enable it with the `-race` flag:

- `go test -race ./...` — the most valuable place; run it in CI.
- `go run -race .` or `go build -race` for manual testing of a binary.

It adds checks around every memory access and reports races that **actually happen during the run**, with stack traces for both accesses and where the goroutines were created. It has no false positives, but it can only find races your tests exercise — so tests should run the concurrent code paths. Expect roughly 5–10× slower execution and more memory; it's for testing, not production builds. It needs cgo (Go's bridge to C code) on most platforms.

Fixing a race means guaranteeing that one access **happens before** the other, so the second sees the first's result:

- Protect the data with a `sync.Mutex`.
- Use `sync/atomic` types for single counters or flags.
- Transfer ownership through a channel so only one goroutine touches the data at a time.
- Give each goroutine its own data, such as its own slice index, and combine after `wg.Wait()`.

"It's only a counter, the occasional wrong value is fine" is not a valid excuse — racy programs have no guaranteed behaviour at all.
takeaways: A race = concurrent access, one write, no synchronisation
`go test -race ./...` in CI; it finds races that occur during the run
Fix with mutexes, atomics, channels or not sharing at all
pitfalls: Assuming no race report means no races — the detector only sees code paths that ran concurrently.

quiz.q: The race detector reports nothing for your test suite. What can you conclude?
options: No races occurred in the executions the tests performed
Only that there are no map races
quiz.explain: It only sees races that actually happen while the tests run, so code the tests don't run concurrently may still race.

concepts.name: Benchmarks and pprof profiling
concepts.summary: Measure performance with testing benchmarks and benchstat, then find hot spots with CPU and memory profiles.
concepts.why: Optimising without measuring wastes time; Go's built-in benchmarks and pprof make measuring easy.
concepts.body:
A **benchmark** is a function `func BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B)` in a `_test.go` file. Run the code under test `b.N` times; the framework increases `b.N` until timing is stable:

```go
for range b.N { Parse(input) }
```

(Go 1.24 adds `for b.Loop() { ... }`, which also prevents the compiler from optimising the work away and excludes setup automatically.)

Run with `go test -bench=. -benchmem`. Output shows ns/op (nanoseconds per run of your code), and with `-benchmem` also B/op and allocs/op — bytes and memory allocations per run, which are often the real cost. Use `b.ReportAllocs()`, `b.ResetTimer()` after expensive setup, and sub-benchmarks with `b.Run` to compare sizes. Results are noisy: run with `-count=10` before and after a change and compare with **benchstat** (`golang.org/x/perf/cmd/benchstat`), which tells you whether a difference is real or just noise.

To find *where* time goes, use a **profiler**; Go's is **pprof**:

- `go test -bench=Parse -cpuprofile cpu.out -memprofile mem.out`
- `go tool pprof -http=:8081 cpu.out` opens a web page with **flame graphs**, the top functions and annotated source code.
- In a running service, `import _ "net/http/pprof"` registers `/debug/pprof/` handlers. Then `go tool pprof http://host:port/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30` grabs a CPU profile; `/heap`, `/goroutine`, `/mutex` and `/block` show other views. Don't expose these endpoints publicly.

`go tool trace` shows a timeline of what every goroutine and the garbage collector did, when profiles aren't enough. And **profile-guided optimisation**: put a typical CPU profile at `default.pgo` in the main package, and `go build` uses it to speed up the code that runs most (the **hot path**), typically gaining a few percent.
takeaways: `BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B)` + `go test -bench=. -benchmem`
Compare runs with benchstat, not by eyeballing one result
pprof (files or net/http/pprof) shows where CPU and memory go
pitfalls: Benchmarking code whose result is unused, letting the compiler eliminate the work you meant to measure.

quiz.q: Which flag adds allocation statistics (B/op, allocs/op) to benchmark output?
quiz.explain: -benchmem reports memory allocation stats for every benchmark.

concepts.name: Reflection with reflect
concepts.summary: Inspect types and values at run time with reflect.TypeOf and ValueOf, read struct tags, and set fields.
concepts.why: Reflection powers encoding/json and libraries that read your structs' fields automatically; you need it to write such tools and to understand them.
concepts.body:
**Reflection** means a program examining its own values and types while it runs. Go's `reflect` package lets code handle values whose type it doesn't know when it's written. It starts from an interface value:

- `reflect.TypeOf(x)` returns a `reflect.Type`: its `Name()`, `Kind()` (Struct, Slice, Ptr, Int…), and for structs `NumField()` and `Field(i)`, which includes the field's name and **tag** (`f.Tag.Get("json")`).
- `reflect.ValueOf(x)` returns a `reflect.Value` holding the data, with accessors like `Int()`, `String()`, `Len()`, `Index(i)`, `Field(i)`, `MapRange()`.

**Kind vs Type**: a `type UserID int` has Type `UserID` but Kind `Int`. Generic reflection code switches on Kind.

To **modify** a value through reflection you need a value Go can write back to, which means reaching it through a pointer: pass a pointer and call `Elem()`, as in `reflect.ValueOf(&cfg).Elem()`. `v.CanSet()` reports whether setting is allowed; unexported fields are readable but not settable. Calling `SetInt` on a non-settable value, or `Int()` on a non-integer Kind, **panics** — reflection trades compile-time checks for run-time panics.

The Laws of Reflection summarise it: reflection goes from interface value to reflection object and back (`v.Interface()`), and to modify a reflection object the value must be settable.

Costs: reflective code is slower (often 10–100× for field access), allocates, and is harder to read. Prefer interfaces, generics or code generation (`go generate`, which writes Go code for you before building) when they fit, and keep reflection at the edges — encoding and decoding, **dependency injection** (handing parts of a program what they need automatically), test helpers. Remember what you learn about each type, such as parsed tags, since inspecting a Type again and again is wasteful.
takeaways: TypeOf for type info (Kind, fields, tags), ValueOf for data
To set via reflection, start from a pointer and call Elem()
Reflection errors are run-time panics; keep it at the edges
pitfalls: Calling reflect.ValueOf(cfg) (not &cfg) and then trying to set a field — it panics because it's only a copy, which Go won't let you change.

quiz.q: `type Celsius float64; var c Celsius` — what is `reflect.TypeOf(c).Kind()`?
quiz.explain: Kind is the underlying category of the type; the named type Celsius has Kind Float64.

concepts.name: The scheduler: G, M and P
concepts.summary: How the Go runtime shares goroutines among operating-system threads: run queues, work stealing, system calls and preemption.
concepts.why: Understanding the scheduler explains goroutine costs, GOMAXPROCS tuning, and odd latency or CPU behaviour.
concepts.body:
The **Go scheduler**, part of the runtime, decides which goroutine runs where. It juggles three kinds of things:

- **G** — a goroutine: its stack, instruction pointer and status.
- **M** — a machine, i.e. an OS thread that executes code.
- **P** — a processor: the right to run Go code, plus a local run queue of runnable Gs. There are exactly `GOMAXPROCS` Ps.

An M must hold a P to run Go code, so `GOMAXPROCS` caps how many goroutines execute Go code simultaneously. It defaults to the number of CPUs; since Go 1.25 it also respects the CPU limit of a container it runs in, which older versions ignored (hence the popular `automaxprocs` package).

Scheduling flow: `go f()` puts the new G in the current P's local queue (in a `runnext` slot, so it tends to run soon). When a P's queue empties it checks the global queue, then the network, and then **steals half** of another P's queue — this is **work stealing**. This keeps all cores busy without a central lock.

Blocking is handled differently by cause:

- Channel, mutex or sleep: the G is parked and the M simply runs another G — cheap.
- Network I/O: the G parks on the **netpoller**, which uses the operating system's "tell me when data arrives" features (epoll, kqueue, IOCP), and is made runnable when the socket is ready, so thousands of connections need only a few threads.
- Blocking syscalls and cgo calls: the M is stuck, so the P is handed off to another M (the `sysmon` background thread retakes it if the call takes too long). This is why heavy blocking file I/O or cgo can create many threads.

Since Go 1.14 the runtime can **preempt** a goroutine — pause it from outside — at almost any point: sysmon signals a goroutine that has run for about 10ms, so tight loops can no longer hog a P or hold up the garbage collector. `GODEBUG=schedtrace=1000` prints scheduler state every second, and `go tool trace` visualises it.
takeaways: G = goroutine, M = OS thread, P = execution slot; GOMAXPROCS Ps
Idle Ps steal work; network I/O parks on the netpoller, not a thread
Blocking syscalls/cgo pin an M; preemption is asynchronous since 1.14
pitfalls: Setting GOMAXPROCS far above the container's CPU quota on old Go versions, causing throttling and latency spikes.

quiz.q: A goroutine blocks reading from a TCP socket. What happens to its OS thread (M)?
options: The thread blocks until data arrives
The goroutine is parked on the netpoller and the thread runs other goroutines
The runtime spins the thread until data is ready
quiz.explain: Network I/O is non-blocking under the hood; the G parks and the M continues with other work.

quiz.q: What does GOMAXPROCS limit?
options: The number of OS threads the process may create
How many goroutines can execute Go code at the same time
The size of each goroutine's stack
quiz.explain: It sets the number of Ps; threads blocked in syscalls don't hold a P, so the thread count can exceed it.

concepts.name: The Go memory model
concepts.summary: Happens-before, what synchronisation guarantees visibility, and why racy programs have no reliable meaning.
concepts.why: Correct lock-free and concurrent code depends on exactly which operations order memory between goroutines.
concepts.body:
The Go **memory model** is the set of rules that answers one question: when is a goroutine guaranteed to see a write made by another? Without synchronisation, never — compilers and CPUs reorder and cache memory operations freely, as long as a single goroutine can't tell.

Guarantees come from **happens-before** edges created by synchronising operations:

- `go f()` happens before `f` starts.
- A send on a channel happens before the corresponding receive completes; closing a channel happens before a receive that returns because it's closed.
- For an unbuffered channel, a receive happens before the matching send completes. Generally, the k-th receive on a channel with capacity C happens before the (k+C)-th send completes — which is why a buffered channel works as a semaphore.
- `mu.Unlock()` happens before the next `mu.Lock()` returns. `once.Do(f)`: f's completion happens before any `Do` returns. `wg.Done` happens before the `Wait` it unblocks.
- `sync/atomic` operations are **sequentially consistent** — every goroutine sees them in one agreed order: if an atomic load observes an atomic store, the store happens before the load.

Happens-before is transitive, so writes before a send are visible after the receive.

Since the 2022 revision (Go 1.19), Go promises **DRF-SC** (data-race-free means sequentially consistent): a program without data races behaves as if its goroutines simply took turns on one CPU core. With a race, guarantees mostly evaporate. Single-word races only expose some value that was written, but races on strings, slices, interfaces or maps can expose half-written values and corrupt memory.

The classic broken approach is a plain `bool` "ready" flag checked by a loop that spins until it's set: the reader may never see the update, or see the flag before the data. Use a channel, a mutex, or an `atomic.Bool` — then both the flag and the data written before it become visible.
takeaways: Visibility across goroutines requires a happens-before edge
Channels, mutexes, Once, WaitGroup and atomics create those edges
Race-free programs are sequentially consistent; racy ones have no reliable meaning
pitfalls: Publishing data with a plain bool flag and a spin loop — the reader may never see it, or see stale data.

quiz.q: Goroutine A writes x = 1 then sends on unbuffered channel c. Goroutine B receives from c then reads x. What does B see?
quiz.explain: The write precedes the send, the send happens before the receive completes, and the receive precedes the read — so x = 1 is visible.

concepts.name: Escape analysis and allocation
concepts.summary: How the compiler decides between stack and heap, how to read -gcflags=-m output, and ways to cut memory allocations.
concepts.why: Heap allocations are what the garbage collector has to clean up; knowing what escapes lets you fix busy code with evidence instead of guesses.
concepts.body:
A function's values can live in two places. **The stack** is each goroutine's own scratch memory: a value there is freed automatically, at no cost, when the function returns. The **heap** is shared memory that the garbage collector must clean up later.

Go doesn't let you choose — the compiler does, through **escape analysis**. A value stays on the stack if the compiler can prove nothing still refers to it after the call. Otherwise it **escapes** to the heap.

See the decisions with `go build -gcflags=-m ./...` (add a second `-m` for reasons). You'll see lines like `moved to heap: x`, `&T{...} escapes to heap` and `p does not escape`.

Common reasons a value escapes:

- Its address is returned, or stored in a global, a heap object, or a channel.
- It's converted to an **interface** and the compiler can't see what the called function does with it — passing values to `fmt.Println` is the classic case.
- A closure captures it and the closure itself escapes (e.g. it's started with `go`).
- Its size isn't known when compiling, like `make([]byte, n)` where `n` is only known at run time, or it's very large.

Function **inlining** — the compiler copying a small function's body into its caller — matters: when a small constructor is inlined, its result may no longer escape. `-gcflags=-m` also reports what was inlined.

Goroutine stacks start small and grow by **copying** to a bigger stack, so the runtime updates pointers into the stack. That's one reason Go pointers to stack memory can't be handed to C code.

Techniques for hot paths, once a profile proves they matter:

- Let callers pass in buffers (`Append`-style APIs such as `strconv.AppendInt`) instead of returning new slices.
- Preallocate slices and maps with known sizes.
- Reuse temporary objects with `sync.Pool`.
- Avoid interface conversions and `fmt` in inner loops.

Measure with `-benchmem` or `testing.AllocsPerRun`; don't distort clean code for allocations that don't show up in a profile.
takeaways: The compiler puts a value on the heap only if it may outlive its function
`-gcflags=-m` shows escape and inlining decisions
Interfaces, captured variables and returned pointers are common escape causes
pitfalls: Micro-optimising away allocations that never appear in a profile, making code harder to read for no gain.

quiz.q: Why does `fmt.Println(x)` usually make x escape?
options: fmt copies all arguments to a global buffer
Printing requires heap memory for strings
Println runs in a new goroutine
x is converted to an interface (any) passed to a function the compiler can't prove doesn't retain it
quiz.explain: Arguments become `any` values, and the analysis must assume the called function may keep them, so their data goes to the heap.

concepts.name: The garbage collector and GOGC
concepts.summary: How Go's concurrent mark-sweep GC works, the GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT knobs, and how to observe and tune it.
concepts.why: GC behaviour sets your service's CPU overhead, memory use and its slowest response times.
concepts.body:
Go's collector is **mark-and-sweep**: it marks every value the program can still reach, then frees the rest. It doesn't sort values by age (it's *non-generational*) and never moves them in memory (*non-moving*), which keeps pointers stable and makes sharing memory with C simpler. Most marking runs concurrently with your code; only two short **stop-the-world** pauses bracket it, usually well under a millisecond. While marking, a **write barrier** notes every pointer change, so running code can't hide a value that's still in use.

When does a cycle start? The **heap goal** is controlled by `GOGC` (default 100): after a collection, the next one triggers when the heap grows by GOGC% of the live heap — the memory still in use after the last collection — (plus the memory the collector always scans, such as goroutine stacks and global variables). With 100 MB live, the next GC targets about 200 MB.

- Higher `GOGC` → fewer cycles, less CPU, more memory. `GOGC=off` disables collection.
- `GOMEMLIMIT` (Go 1.19+) is a **soft memory limit**: as total runtime memory approaches it, the GC runs more often regardless of GOGC. Setting it a bit below a container's memory limit, often combined with a higher GOGC, avoids the program being killed for running out of memory (OOM) while keeping GC cheap.
- Both can be set from code via `runtime/debug.SetGCPercent` and `SetMemoryLimit`.

If allocation outpaces marking, the runtime makes allocating goroutines do **mark assist** work, which shows up as latency. GC cost scales mainly with the amount of live, pointer-containing memory and the allocation rate — so reducing allocations is the most effective tuning.

Observe it with `GODEBUG=gctrace=1` (one line per cycle), `runtime.ReadMemStats`, the `runtime/metrics` package, and the GC lanes in `go tool trace`. Go 1.24 added `runtime.AddCleanup` and the `weak` package as better alternatives to `runtime.SetFinalizer` (code that runs when a value is collected); Go 1.25 shipped the experimental "Green Tea" collector, which marks memory in a more cache-friendly order.
takeaways: Concurrent, non-moving, non-generational mark-sweep with a write barrier
GOGC trades CPU for memory; GOMEMLIMIT caps memory softly
Fewer allocations and less live pointer data = cheaper GC
pitfalls: Setting GOMEMLIMIT below the program's actual live heap — the GC runs continuously and the program crawls (thrashing).

quiz.q: Live heap is 50 MB and GOGC=100. Roughly when will the next collection be triggered?
quiz.explain: The heap goal is live heap × (1 + GOGC/100) = 100 MB, plus a little for stacks and global variables.

concepts.name: Interface internals: itabs and nil
concepts.summary: How interface values are stored (itab or type, plus data), the cost of boxing and indirect calls, and the typed-nil trap.
concepts.why: These internals explain interface allocations, comparison panics and the famous non-nil nil error.
concepts.body:
An interface value is two machine words — two pointer-sized slots:

- An **empty interface** (`any`, `eface` in the runtime) holds a pointer to the **type descriptor** (the runtime's record of a type: its size, name and methods) and a pointer to the **data**.
- A **non-empty interface** (`iface`) holds a pointer to an **itab** and the data pointer. The itab records the interface type, the concrete type, and a table of function pointers for the interface's methods, in a fixed order. Itabs are computed once and cached.

A method call through an interface looks up the method's address in the itab and calls it there — an **indirect call**. It's cheap but can't be inlined, which is the real cost. When the compiler can see the concrete type it can sometimes call the method directly instead (**devirtualise**), and profile-guided optimisation does this for frequently used calls.

The data word must be a pointer. Storing a pointer-shaped value (a pointer, map, channel or func) in an interface is free; storing anything else — an `int`, a struct, a string — normally **boxes** it: the value is copied to the heap and the interface points at the copy. The runtime avoids allocation for zero-sized values, single-byte values and constants, but in hot code repeated boxing shows up in profiles.

Consequences:

- An interface equals `nil` only when its type word is nil. A `var p *MyErr = nil` returned as `error` has a type word, so `err != nil` is **true**. Return a literal `nil`.
- Comparing interfaces compares the types, then the values with the type's `==`. If the dynamic type is not comparable (a slice, map or func), `==` **panics at run time**, including when used as a map key.
- Type assertion to a concrete type is a single pointer comparison; assertion to another interface needs an itab lookup.
takeaways: Interfaces are (itab or type, data pointer) pairs
Non-pointer values are usually boxed on the heap when stored in an interface
nil interface ≠ interface holding a nil pointer; uncomparable dynamic types panic on ==
pitfalls: Declaring `var err *MyErr` and returning it as `error` — callers always see a non-nil error.

quiz.q: `var a, b any = map[string]int{}, map[string]int{}` — what does `a == b` do?
quiz.explain: The comparison compiles because both are `any`, but the type stored inside, a map, can't be compared, so it panics at run time.

concepts.name: unsafe and cgo
concepts.summary: Step outside the type system with unsafe.Pointer, follow its rules, and call C code with cgo at a known cost.
concepts.why: Low-level libraries, zero-copy conversions and calling C code need these tools — and their rules are strict.
concepts.body:
Go normally guarantees **type safety**: memory holding an `int` is only ever used as an `int`. The **unsafe** package lets you step around that. `unsafe.Sizeof`, `Alignof` and `Offsetof` describe how a struct is laid out in memory; fields may need gaps (padding) between them, so reordering fields can shrink a struct.

`unsafe.Pointer` can be converted to and from any pointer type and to `uintptr`, a plain integer the size of a pointer — but only in the patterns listed in its documentation. Examples: converting `*T1` to `*T2` when both have the same layout, or pointer arithmetic within **one expression**: `unsafe.Pointer(uintptr(p) + off)`. The garbage collector doesn't treat a `uintptr` as a pointer, so storing one in a variable and converting it back later is a bug.

Since Go 1.20, `unsafe.String`, `unsafe.StringData`, `unsafe.Slice` and `unsafe.SliceData` give an approved way to convert without copying (**zero-copy**) between `[]byte` and `string`. The contract: the bytes must never be modified afterwards, since strings are assumed immutable. Code using unsafe may break across Go versions and isn't covered by Go's promise that old code keeps working; `go vet` catches some misuse.

**cgo** lets Go call code written in the C language. A comment directly above `import "C"` holds C code or `#include` lines, and you call `C.func(...)`:

```go
// #include <stdlib.h>
import "C"
cs := C.CString("hi") // malloc'd copy
defer C.free(unsafe.Pointer(cs))
```

Costs and rules:

- Each call crosses from Go to C, costing far more than a Go call, and it ties up an operating-system thread while it runs — do a lot of work per call.
- C may not keep Go pointers after the call returns, and memory passed to C must not contain Go pointers; `runtime.Pinner` (Go 1.21) pins objects when needed.
- cgo needs a C compiler, and makes building for other systems and producing self-contained executables harder. `CGO_ENABLED=0` gives pure-Go, fully static builds — prefer pure-Go libraries when they exist.
takeaways: unsafe.Pointer conversions are valid only in the documented patterns
Never store a uintptr and convert it back later — the GC can't see it
cgo calls are costly and have pointer-passing rules; CGO_ENABLED=0 for pure-Go builds
pitfalls: Mutating a []byte after converting it to a string with unsafe.String — breaks string immutability and can corrupt map keys.
Forgetting to C.free a C.CString — C memory is not garbage collected.

quiz.q: Why is `u := uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(p)); ...; q := unsafe.Pointer(u)` across statements invalid?
options: uintptr is too small to hold a pointer
The GC doesn't treat u as a reference, so the object may be freed or moved in between
unsafe.Pointer cannot be converted to uintptr
quiz.explain: A uintptr is an integer, not a pointer; only the single-expression patterns keep the object alive and valid.
